mathematics_checks: The revised first displayed equality is correct: global measurability of the total gradient (MeasurableGradient.measurable_gradient) gives a measurable, hence strongly measurable in finite-dimensional Euclidean space, score lift. The measurable first projection pushes γ to μ, so the displayed γ-integral of ‖s(x)‖² equals the μ-integral and I, and the pullback is integrable. This uses the selected function throughout and does not infer differentiability from measurability.

The second display is correct: ‖y − x‖ ≤ ‖x‖ + ‖y‖ and (a + b)² ≤ 2a² + 2b² give the squared bound. Both coordinate norm squares pull back from their respective marginals, and continuous squared displacement dominated by their integrable sum yields finite Cγ ≥ 0 without probability, sigma-finiteness or optimality.

The revised Hölder display is valid and complete: the lifted score and displacement are L², so the product of their norms is integrable. Pointwise inner-product Cauchy–Schwarz dominates the measurable scalar pairing, proving its integrability. The absolute integral is at most the integral of the absolute pairing, then the norm-product integral, then √I √Cγ by L² Hölder. The displayed chain has the correct sign and unit constant and requires no optimality.

The same nonnegative integrand defines the extended cost up to norm_sub_rev; integrability gives ∫⁻ ofReal(‖y − x‖²) dγ = ofReal(Cγ). Only the identification of this cost with the infimum W₂² uses optimality. Since ofReal(Cγ) is finite, W₂ cannot be infinite, and the nonnegative real square root gives √Cγ = W₂.toReal. An arbitrary feasible plan also bounds the infimum above by a finite cost, but W₂ ≤ √Cγ then has the wrong direction to justify the replacement in an upper bound.
